newsitem.title: USA: Continental says merger not imminent.
newsitem.headline: Continental says merger not imminent.

text.p: Continental Airlines executives said Wednesday a merger with Delta Air Lines was not imminent, but they stopped short of denying the two carriers were in talks on a deal that would form the nation's largest airline.

The Houston-based airline's two top executives also defended their recent sale of Continental stock, telling employees the decision to exercise stocks options indicated a merger was not on the horizon.

"We obviously would not have exercised stock options if we thought a merger was right around the corner which would create a windfall for all stockholders," Continental Chairman Gordon Bethune and President Greg Brenneman said in the memo to employees, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.
The New York Times and Wall Street Journal, quoting sources familiar with the talks, reported Continental approached Delta several months ago about a possible merger.
Officials with Delta, the nation's third-largest carrier, declined to comment on the report. A Continental spokesman declined to elaborate on the memo.
The reports of merger talks drove up the stocks of both airlines, but industry analysts said there were better merger partners for both carriers.

"I think Continental is being shopped because there are a lot of investment types that own the stock," said airline analyst Raymond Neidl with Furman Selz in New York. "But there are other carriers that would be a better fit for Continental, like United, Northwest and USAir."
"I'm extremely skeptical. It's highly unlikely that this deal would happen," said Edward Starkman at Dillon Read. "What does Continental bring to the party that Delta dosen't already have?"

Analysts valued Continental at more than $1.8 billion. If a deal were to occur, analysts said it would probably spark a round of consolidation in the domestic airline industry, which has recovered to post solid earnings this year and last after struggling for much of the prior decade.
The likely winners in a Continental-Delta deal would be Fort Worth, Texas-based Air Partners LP, which led an investment of $450 million to help Continental emerge from bankruptcy.

If an agreement is reached, the proposed merger would get tough scrutiny in Washington, where the Justice Department would take a close look at the merger's impact on competition especially at airports with restricted landing slots.
"The ones that are of the most antitrust concern are the airports where no one else can get in, like New York and Washington," said Don Farmer, a Washington antitrust attorney.
The merger talks also came as news to Continental's pilots union, which found itself in the dark as reports surfaced of talks between the two carriers.
"This was all news to the pilots," said Capt. Bob Wilson, president of the Independent Association of Continental Pilots, who planned to meet with company executives this week to discuss the talks.

Approval from the pilot's union was considered a key to completing a deal, and the fact that the union had not yet been consulted could be regarded as a sign that any talks were in the preliminary stages.

Continental's pilots have had a bumpy relationship with the airline since former Chairman Frank Lorenzo put the company into bankruptcy in 1983 and rescinded its labor agreements. The carrier also filed for bankruptcy a second time, in 1990.

But the union signed a new labor pact with Continental in June 1995, and Wilson credited Bethune with reviving the once-ailing airline. "What he did was provide the environment for the employees to bring the airline back from the brink," he said.
Consolidation in the industry has been widely predicted but slow to get off the ground.

USAir Group put itself up for sale a year ago and held talks with United Airlines, the nation's largest carrier, and No. 2 American Airlines. But the talks were later called off. United Airlines is a unit of UAL Corp., and American is owned by AMR Corp.

Analysts said Continental and Delta would fit well geographically, with Continental strong in Houston, the New York area and Latin and central America, and Delta strongth in the Southeast, along the East Coast and in Europe.
Continental's more widely traded class B stock jumped $2.375 to $30.75 and Delta stock added 50 cents to $75.50, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
